title: The Prophets Speak and the Work Resumes
summary: The prophets Haggai and Zechariah stir Zerubbabel and Jeshua to restart the temple. Tattenai, the Persian governor of the province west of the Euphrates, comes to ask who authorized the work, but because the eye of God is on the elders, the building continues while he writes to King Darius. His letter reports the Jews' answer, that Cyrus had decreed the rebuilding, and asks the king to search the royal archives.
story: Chapter 4 ended with the work standing still until the second year of Darius. Chapter 5 opens with that stillness broken, not by a new royal decree but by prophets. The returnees had lived for years with a laid foundation and no temple, discouraged by their neighbors and by their own hardships. Now God's word through Haggai and Zechariah sets them in motion again, and this time the challenge from the Persian authorities, which had stopped them before, becomes the means by which their right to build is confirmed. The chapter creates suspense: Tattenai's letter goes to Darius, and the reader must wait until chapter 6 to learn what the archives will reveal.
historical:
Darius I seized the Persian throne in 522 BC after a period of revolt and spent his first years putting down rebellions across the empire. His second year was 520 BC. The book of Haggai dates his first message to the first day of the sixth month of that year and says work resumed on the twenty-fourth day of the same month (Haggai 1:1, 15); Zechariah began prophesying two months later (Zechariah 1:1). Their messages, preserved in their own books, rebuked the people for living in paneled houses while God's house lay in ruins, and promised God's presence and blessing.

Tattenai was the governor of Beyond the River, the large Persian province west of the Euphrates, of which Judah was a small part. A Babylonian document from the reign of Darius names a Tattannu as governor of that province, very likely the same man. His inquiry looks like the routine work of a careful official: after the upheavals at the start of Darius's reign, an unexplained building project in a city with a history of rebellion would call for a report. Shethar-bozenai, who appears with him, seems to have been a fellow official, perhaps a secretary.
cultural:
In the Persian empire, construction of a temple or fortification required royal permission, and officials were expected to verify it. Tattenai's questions (who authorized this, and what are the names of the builders) were the questions of a regional governor protecting the king's interests and his own position. Recording names meant that if the work proved unauthorized, those responsible could be held accountable.

The elders' reply is notable for its honesty and its theology. They identify themselves as servants of the God of heaven and earth, admit that their own fathers angered God and so brought about the temple's destruction, and then appeal to Cyrus's decree. Before a foreign official they confess that the exile was God's judgment, not a failure of their God. The large stones and timbers described in verse 8 reflect a known ancient building technique in which courses of timber were laid between courses of stone, a method also described for the inner court of Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6:36) and in Cyrus's own specifications (Ezra 6:4).
literary: The chapter is in Aramaic, part of the section running from 4:8 to 6:18, and most of it is a letter quoted in full. The narrative frame (verses 1-5) sets the scene, then Tattenai's report (verses 6-17) repeats the question of verse 3 and records the elders' answer at length. That answer (verses 11-16) is a compact retelling of Israel's history: Solomon's temple, the people's sin, Nebuchadnezzar's destruction, Cyrus's decree, the return of the vessels, and the foundation laid under Sheshbazzar. Through the voice of a Persian official, the reader hears the book's own account of the past. The phrase the eye of their God in verse 5 is the theological hinge: the Persian official is watching, but God is watching more closely.

outline.t: Haggai and Zechariah stir the leaders to rebuild
Tattenai's inquiry, and God's eye on the elders
The elders' answer: the temple's history and Cyrus's decree
A request to search the royal archives

doctrines.note: The work resumes because prophets speak in the name of the God of Israel. The chapter shows the living word of God, not a change in circumstances, as what moves the discouraged community to act.

God's eye is on the elders so that they are not stopped while the report goes to the king. God does not remove the official inquiry; he works through it, keeping the builders at work while the empire's own process runs its course.

The elders tell a foreign governor that their fathers angered God and that the exile was the result. Owning the past honestly, rather than excusing it, is part of how the returned community understands its restoration.

words.note: Ayin, eye, here in Aramaic. The eye of their God was on the elders (verse 5) expresses God's watchful care and protection. Elsewhere in Scripture God's eyes on his people signal favor and attention (Psalm 33:18; 34:15). The phrase answers the watching eye of the Persian governor with the higher watch of God.

Nevi, the Aramaic form of the Hebrew navi, prophet: one who speaks for God. Haggai and Zechariah are named as the prophets who restarted the work and who stayed with the builders, helping them. Their presence shows prophecy in this period not only as warning but as encouragement to a weary people.

Siv, to be gray, used as a noun for elders, those gray-haired with age and experience. In chapters 5 and 6 the elders of the Jews are the community's leaders before the Persian authorities. The term reflects the old Israelite pattern of leadership by the heads of families and clans, which carried on under foreign rule.

christ: The chapter's movement from stalled work to renewed building through the prophetic word has a clear parallel in the New Testament's picture of the church, which is built as a spiritual house on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus as the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:19-22; 1 Peter 2:4-5). That is a development of the temple theme, not a hidden meaning in Ezra 5. More directly, the prophets who speak in this chapter, Haggai and Zechariah, looked beyond the temple of their day. Haggai promised that God would fill the house with glory, and Zechariah spoke of a man called the Branch who would build the temple of the LORD and bear royal honor (Zechariah 6:12-13). Christians have seen those promises, only partly met in Zerubbabel, finding their fullness in Jesus.
questions: The community restarted the work because of God's word rather than a change in their circumstances. What role does hearing God's word play in moving you from discouragement to action?
The elders told a foreign official honestly that their fathers had angered God. How does owning past failure openly change the way a community speaks about its present?
God's eye was on the builders while their case was under review. How might that image shape the way you wait for decisions you cannot control?
